title: AWS Sydney 2016: Voltage Sag Drains the Rotary UPS, One Zone Loses Power
dcName: AWS facility in the Sydney Region (not named)

severity.usersAffected: A significant number of EC2 instances and EBS volumes in one Sydney Availability Zone; launch errors across the Region until failover.

brief: On 4 June 2016 (5 June in Sydney) storms took out a substation and the grid sagged rather than failed. In one AWS facility the breakers isolating the rotary UPS opened too slowly, the flywheel energy drained into the grid and both power line-ups dropped. Power was back in 81 minutes; a recovery bug and storage drive failures stretched customer recovery to about 9.5 hours.

magnitude.note: One Availability Zone in a major region; multi-zone customers stayed up. Duration (5): about 9 h 35 min from trigger to nearly all instances back, inside the 4–12 h band. Cost not disclosed.

rootCause:
TRIGGER: severe weather took out a regional substation at 22:25 PDT on 4 June 2016 (15:25 Sydney time on 5 June). Several AWS facilities lost utility power. The failure did not look like a clean outage: it was an unusually long voltage sag.

POWER CHAIN: in one facility the instances were fed by two independent line-ups, each built on diesel rotary UPS (DRUPS) units, a flywheel plus an integrated diesel generator. To ride through, the DRUPS must be cut off from the grid so its flywheel feeds only the load until the diesel takes over. During the long sag the isolating breakers did not open quickly enough, the flywheel energy drained back into the degraded grid, and the DRUPS shut down. The generators that had started could no longer be connected, so both line-ups were lost together.

RECOVERY CHAIN: power was back at 23:46 PDT, but customer recovery took until about 08:00. Internal DNS struggled under the recovery load, the APIs were slow to show new state, a latent bug in the instance management software stopped automatic recovery of part of the fleet, and drive failures on some storage servers left a very small share of EBS volumes unrecoverable automatically.

LATENT ROOT: the two 'independent' line-ups shared one design and one weakness, so one grid signature defeated both at once, and the recovery tooling had a fault that only a real mass restart could expose.
contributingFactors: The grid fault was a long voltage sag, not a clean outage, so it did not trip the protection the way a dead feed would (AWS summary).
The breakers isolating the DRUPS from the utility did not open quickly enough, and the flywheel energy drained into the grid (AWS summary).
Both power line-ups used the same DRUPS design, so the same sag defeated them together and instances lost primary and secondary power (AWS summary).
A latent bug in the instance management software blocked automatic recovery of part of the fleet (AWS summary).
Some storage servers lost hard drives in the event; volumes with both replicas on failed servers could not be restored automatically (AWS summary).
Instance launch APIs depended on the degraded zone until the team failed them away by hand (AWS summary).
Internal DNS hosts were overloaded by the recovery load after power returned (AWS summary).

coe.action: Add breakers so connections to degraded utility power are broken faster and generators engage before the UPS energy is used up
Fix the latent bug that stopped automatic recovery of some instances
coe.status: In testing at the time of the summary; deployment over the following days

coe.action: Start a program to test recovery processes regularly on unoccupied long-running hosts
Make the instance launch APIs more resilient to a zone failure, with roll-out to the Sydney Region in July 2016
Manual failover of launch APIs away from the degraded zone
Manual recovery of the remaining instances and of damaged storage servers

lessonsLearnt: Two power line-ups are only independent if they fail in different ways. Same DRUPS design on both sides means one grid signature can take both.
Protection must be tested against the grid's real failure shapes, including long sags, not only a clean loss of supply.
A rotary UPS has seconds of stored energy; anything that lets that energy leak back into the grid turns ride-through into a trip.
Mass recovery after a power loss exercises code paths that daily operation never touches; test them deliberately and often.
Control-plane APIs must not depend on the zone that has failed; failing them away by hand cost over an hour of launch errors.
Customers running across several Availability Zones stayed up; single-zone workloads carried the whole outage.
improvements: Design: additional breakers to isolate degraded utility power faster (AWS committed).
Software: fix the latent instance-recovery bug (AWS, in testing at the time).
Process: regular recovery tests on unoccupied long-running hosts (AWS committed).
Control plane: more resilient launch APIs, Sydney roll-out planned for July 2016 (AWS).
Analyst recommendation (not in the summary): test UPS isolation logic against recorded sag profiles from the local grid, and avoid identical protection designs on both line-ups.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: A sag, not a blackout
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: A dead feed is the easy case for protection. A long sag leaves enough voltage that the input breaker logic hesitates, and a flywheel UPS has only seconds of energy to spend. The design worked well for years and failed on a waveform it had not been built for.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Common-mode failure across two line-ups
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Every instance had two independent line-ups. Both used the same DRUPS scheme, so the same sag defeated both. Redundancy counts only against failures that do not hit every copy the same way.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: The long tail was software
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Power returned 81 minutes after the trigger, but nearly all instances were back only after about nine and a half hours. DNS load, slow API state, a latent recovery bug and storage drive failures each added time.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Multi-zone design held
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: AWS notes that customers running across several Availability Zones kept their applications available. The event is a clear case for spreading critical workloads across zones.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: What the summary does not say
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: It does not name the facility, the DRUPS make, the breaker type, how many instances were affected or the cost. It also does not report when the added breakers were installed.

technicalDeepDive:
A DRUPS bridges a utility loss with flywheel energy while its diesel starts. That only works if the unit is islanded from the grid the moment the grid is bad. A clean outage opens the input breaker almost at once; a long sag keeps the voltage just high enough that the breaker logic waits, and in that time the flywheel discharges into the faulted network instead of the load. When the flywheel speed falls too far the DRUPS trips, and the running diesel has nothing to synchronise to.

AWS's fix is in the protection scheme: more breakers so the system breaks from degraded utility power faster. The recovery problems are a separate lesson: a mass power-on drives load patterns (DNS, instance state, storage re-replication) that ordinary operation never exercises, so recovery paths must be tested on purpose.
